banter: Engines don’t lie, detective. Drivers do it professionally.
You can learn a lot from how someone parks and how fast they pretend they didn’t.
Some people leave parking tickets. Others leave entire stories under their wipers.
If a driver backs into a spot perfectly, I immediately wonder what else they’ve rehearsed.
Keys, dents, and fuel receipts make better witnesses than most people I meet.
Everyone thinks they’re the main character until I see how they handle a tight space.
You’d be surprised how many suspects try to escape in a car they can’t parallel park.
repeatLines: We already went over this car, detective.
It hasn’t moved, and neither has the story.
Back again?
The only thing that changed is the parking fee.
I told you what I saw.
If the tyres had more to add, I’d let you know.
No new clues.
Same skid marks, same driver, same bad decisions.
We’ve checked this spot already.
Any more and I’ll start charging you by the minute.
Still the same facts, detective.
Engines don’t rewrite their alibis overnight.
You already emptied this lot of secrets.
Now you’re just circling for comfort.
I gave you everything that would hold up in a report.
The rest is just noise from bad mufflers.
No fresh tyre tracks, no fresh evidence.
Just new stains on old asphalt.
Same parking attendant, same case, same truth.
If you want a different answer, try a different car.
falseLeadLines: You parked your hopes in the wrong spot.
I’ve seen better judgement in people who block fire lanes.
Just other drivers pretending the rules don’t apply to them.
Like a car with the handbrake still on.

At least you didn’t get towed for it.
The thief wasn’t in that city.
Only your optimism was parked there for a while.

You drove a long way for nothing.
That detour didn’t help the case.

london: Your suspect left a rental with a steering wheel on the ‘wrong’ side and asked if all those red buses are really necessary.
They complained about tight parking, then said it reminded them of a city where old stone, fog and impatient taxis fight for the same roads.
Their GPS history mentioned a river, a palace, and more roundabouts than any sane person needs.
paris: They parked like they’d seen too many narrow streets and not enough indicators.
In the glove compartment I saw a parking stub with an iron tower doodled next to a baguette. Subtle, but not subtle enough.
They asked if we validate tickets for a city where scooters, cafés and bad parking form an unofficial national sport.
berlin: They lined up the car with military precision and asked if this city has as many rules as the one with the famous gate.
I heard them mutter about a place that knocked down a wall, painted the pieces and now charges tourists to park near them.
Their dashboard map had a big circle around a district known for serious museums by day and louder engines at night.
new_york_city: They stared at the parking fees and said it still beats hunting for a spot in a city of skyscrapers and yellow taxis.
Your suspect asked if we ever tow cars as fast as they do in the ‘concrete jungle’. I took that as a confession of experience.
There was a crumpled ticket on the seat mentioning a street grid so tight even the pigeons double-park.
warsaw: They parked crooked, then asked if this town also fines people for blocking tram lines and royal views.
On the dashboard I saw a souvenir with a mermaid and a note about a capital that rebuilt its streets more than once.
They said they liked cities where old cobblestones, new office towers and stubborn drivers share the same intersections.
new_delhi: Their car smelled like dust and spices, and they asked if we’ve ever seen traffic as wild as in that big capital further east.
They complained our lot was chaotic, then showed me a photo of an intersection where even scooters look brave.
Your suspect asked if honking is illegal here, because in the city they mentioned it sounds like a national language.

banter: In London, people park like they’re apologising to the curb.
I’ve seen drivers spend ten minutes lining up and still call it ‘good enough’.
The tickets here fear the rain more than the drivers fear the tickets.
repeatLines: We already talked, detective.
Since then, only the drizzle has changed.
Back again?
Same car, same spot, same bad idea.
No new clues.
Just more damp footprints and patient taxis.
falseLeadLines: Even the parking meters knew that wasn’t right.
That lead stalled on the wrong street.
Next time, trust the map, not the mood.
Only confused tourists and angry cab drivers.

banter: Paris drivers treat lanes like suggestions and mirrors like décor.
I’ve seen cars here park closer than most relationships.
The horns sound angry, but that’s just how they say hello.
repeatLines: We already went over this.
No new tyre marks, just new cigarette ash.
Back so soon?
The cars changed, the chaos stayed the same.
No fresh clues.
Only the same dents and better stories.
falseLeadLines: Just scooters, tourists, and bad decisions.

banter: In Berlin, people park like they’re being graded.

Engines may be loud, but the parking is disciplined.
repeatLines: We already checked this car.

No new evidence.

banter: New York drivers park like the world ends in ten minutes.

repeatLines: Yeah, we already talked, detective.

banter: Warsaw drivers park between history and roadworks.

repeatLines: We already discussed this car.

banter: In New Delhi, parking is more negotiation than manoeuvre.

Everyone honks like they’re the main character and the road agrees.
repeatLines: We already talked, detective.

falseLeadLines: Like a car trapped in the wrong lane forever.
